title: Alan Milburn says his plan to get young people into work will save only £200m a year
summary: Author of long-awaited report says money saved in benefit cuts will mostly be used to fund new job support system

blocks.text: Alan Milburn has said his plan to get more young people into work will save the government only £200m a year as the cost of job support swallows up almost all of the anticipated cuts to benefits.

The former health secretary unveiled his long-awaited report into youth unemployment on Tuesday morning, urging ministers to cut disability and sickness payments for under-25s and invest the money in back-to-work schemes. Figures contained in the report show that his plan will not deliver significant overall savings.

The figures are likely to be seized on by the Conservatives as evidence that Labour is not serious about reducing the welfare bill – something the opposition party has put at the heart of its economic policy.

But they will bolster the arguments of Milburn and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, that the year-long review has not been motivated by cuts. “The system I propose will spend less on compensating for economic inactivity, more on creating routes out of it; less on the consequences of failure and more on avoiding it,” Milburn said in the report.

He told Labour MPs at a meeting on Monday night: “The Tories will say it’s too expensive, you can cut faster. But you can’t – or you’d drive young people into destitution with poor housing and ill health.”

Milburn’s report, the outlines of which have been widely trailed over the past few weeks, sets out in detail what he thinks should be done to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).

The plan would involve the government spending nearly £2bn a year on a new youth opportunity service, which would provide support and advice to give every young person a guaranteed route into education, training or work.
It would involve spending just over £2bn to create more vocational training courses and apprenticeships, and a further £1bn in direct payments and tax breaks for companies that hire young people.

The new system would be paid for largely by taking disability and sickness benefits away from young people and replacing them with a single youth allowance, which would be considerably below what some people can claim currently.

People aged 18-24 would no longer be able to claim personal independence payments, which would be replaced by a new allowance available only to those whose conditions are “well established, significant and ongoing”.

The benefits cuts would be expected to save £3.6bn by 2036-37, with an additional £2.4bn being generated by higher tax receipts. That money would be almost entirely swallowed by the £5.8bn cost of the new system, Milburn said.

Milburn began his review last year amid concern at the top of government over the rising numbers of young Neets. That figure reached 1m earlier this year, equating to 13% of young people – a higher rate than in any European country except Romania.
In his report, he argues: “Our country is at a fork in the road. Go on as we are and see the Neet crisis grow. Or change course and make the difficult changes that can shift the trajectory.”

He says his proposals constitute a wholesale rethinking of how the benefits and education system works for young people, and should not be cherrypicked by ministers looking to impose only the ones they like.

He has received public backing from the governments of Burnham and his predecessor, Keir Starmer. When he addressed Labour MPs on Monday he was accompanied by the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden. McFadden and Burnham will speak to the parliamentary party about the plans again on Tuesday morning.

Ministers are hoping they can avoid a repeat of last year’s bruising welfare rebellion, when Labour MPs forced Starmer to drop his plan to cut benefits by about £5bn a year. That humiliation arguably spelled the beginning of the end of Starmer’s time in office. Several of the architects of the rebellion now have government jobs, including the de facto deputy prime minister, Louise Haigh, and the chief whip, Anneliese Midgley.
